item.title: Transferable, Time-Parallel Graph Dynamics via Space-Time Factorization
item.description: arXiv:2611.31479v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Time-parallel neural operators (FNO and successors) have transformed PDE surrogates on regular grids. Mesh-based operators (MeshGraphNets, Transolver) extend operator learning to irregular geometries, but jointly learning across diverse topologies while retaining non-recurrent temporal evaluation remains challenging. We propose space-time factorization: partition the model into local temporal operators (learned, graph-independent) and a spatial mixer that propagates information across nodes without graph-dependent learned parameters. This structural condition lets the same parameters run on unseen graphs; non-recurrent instances also admit time-parallel evaluation. Accurate zero-shot transfer further depends on controlling three information leaks (graph-dependent weights, graph-specific features, and graph-correlated training distributions) and on suitable task physics and training coverage. The protocol applies to two distinct spatial-mixer families, fixed-spectral and learned-attention. We validate the principle in three domains. For floodwave propagation in river networks, a 27K-parameter model trained on the Yangtze transfers zero-shot to the Mississippi with median NSE 0.998 in boundary-conditioned operational evaluation, training 5.5x faster than a stabilized recurrent baseline. On cross-geometry Navier-Stokes, the three-seed SepFNO mean relative vorticity error on five unseen targets falls by about 28% from 5 to 12 training geometries, with a consistent single-run SepTransolver trend. On cross-city traffic forecasting, zero-shot transfer reaches within 12.9% of an oracle trained on the target city. Across settings, cross-geometry error decreases with both the number of training geometries and their relatedness to the test, at a rate depending on the spatial mixer. This opens the path to pooled-data, foundation-style models for graph dynamics on irregular topologies.
item.dc:creator: Wencong Yang, Chaopeng Shen, Abdolmehdi Behroozi

item.title: Effect of humidity and phase transition on turbulent diffusion of droplets and water vapour in atmospheric turbulent flows
item.description: arXiv:2611.32703v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate the effect of humidity on turbulent diffusion of droplets and water vapour in atmospheric turbulent flows taking into account the effect of phase transitions on turbulent transport. We find that the coefficients of turbulent diffusion of droplets and water vapour decrease with increase the turbulent Damk\"{o}hler number (the ratio of turbulent time in the integral scale and phase transition time for condensation of water vapour), while the coefficients of the mutual turbulent diffusion that describe the turbulent cross effects increase with this parameter. For large turbulent Damk\"{o}hler number, the coefficient of turbulent diffusion of droplets is strongly depleted when the evaporation of droplets is much faster than the condensation of water vapour. The obtained theoretical relationships are potentially useful in modelling applications in the atmospheric turbulence.
item.dc:creator: I. Rogachevskii, N. Kleeorin

item.title: Multispectral representation of Distributed Acoustic Sensing data: a framework for physically interpretable feature extraction and visualization
item.description: arXiv:2604.07290v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) enables continuous monitoring of dynamic strain along tens of kilometres of optical fibre, generating massive datasets whose interpretation and automated analysis remain challenging. DAS data can be understood as a time-distance image array. However, the absence of standardised representation methods limits both the physical interpretability and the development of automated image-based analysis pipelines. This work introduces a systematic framework for visualisation and feature extraction of DAS data based on a multispectral signal representation. The approach decomposes strain-rate measurements into predefined frequency bands and produces band-limited energy images that describe the spatial and temporal distribution of acoustic energy across distinct spectral regimes. The framework is evaluated using DAS recordings containing fin whale and blue whale vocalisations. Three experiments are conducted to assess the approach: enhanced visualisation of bioacoustic signals, unsupervised clustering of acoustic patterns, and event detection using a convolutional neural network. The visualisation experiment shows that the multispectral representation allows for the simultaneous visualisation of sets of events that cannot be visualised using the strain amplitude representation. The unsupervised clustering experiment confirms that the multispectral representation yields class-discriminative feature spaces without requiring labelled data, enabling the automatic grouping of acoustically distinct event types. Finally, the use of multispectral composites as input of a ResNet-18 achieves an accuracy of 95.9% in whale vocalisation detection, demonstrating that the proposed representation provides an effective feature space for automated analysis.
item.dc:creator: Sergio Morell-Monz\'o, D\'idac Diego-Tortosa, Isabel P\'erez-Arjona, V\'ictor Espinosa

item.title: ClimTip-GML: A global bias-corrected and downscaled dataset for assessing impacts of climate tipping events
item.description: arXiv:2609.23149v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Assessing the impacts of future climate scenarios including tipping events of major Earth system components such as the Amazon rainforest (ARF) or the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC), requires accurate and high-resolution simulations. Here, we present ClimTip-GML, the first globally bias-corrected and downscaled climate dataset for impact assessment of large-scale tipping scenarios, comprising eight key variables at 0.25{\deg} spatial resolution from three general circulation models (GCMs): CESM1-CAM5, HadGEM3-GC31-MM, and MPI-ESM1-2-HR. The dataset includes 100-year-long climate simulations with preindustrial and historical conditions, as well as scenarios at a +2{\deg}C warming level with and without tipping transitions of the AMOC or ARF. We apply generative machine learning (GML) techniques trained on reanalysis data to bias-correct and downscale the GCMs in a manner that is physically consistent across space, time, and all eight variables. Comprehensive validation shows substantially reduced biases, improved small-scale spatial variability, multivariate correlations, and consistent long-term climate responses to the external forcing and tipping events. The results hence permit substantially improved impact assessments of tipping transitions of the ARF and AMOC, directly informing mitigation and adaptation policies.
item.dc:creator: Philipp Hess, Sebastian Bathiany, Lucas Ferreira Correa, Laura C. Jackson, Casey R. Patrizio, Niklas Boers
